cues.text: We now come to the final chapter of this study session: future trends and sustained compliance.
The question here is how an organisation keeps protecting personal data well, as technology changes and as legal expectations continue to develop.
Let us begin with privacy-enhancing technologies.
The source lists five: differential privacy, federated learning, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, and synthetic data.
These are technical tools designed to let organisations use data while reducing the exposure of individuals.
But, as we will see, each one comes with qualifications, and none of them should be treated as a magic solution.
First, differential privacy.
This technique limits how much any one individual's data can influence an aggregate output.
In other words, if you publish a statistic or a result calculated from many people's records, the result should look almost the same whether or not any single person's data was included.

The source notes that this is often achieved through calibrated noise, meaning a carefully measured amount of random variation is added, so that individuals cannot easily be singled out from the output.
Second, federated learning.
Here, the raw training data stays local, on the device or at the site where it was created, rather than being gathered into one central place.
That is a real privacy advantage.
But the source adds an important caution: the updates that are shared back may still leak information.
So keeping data local does not, by itself, guarantee that nothing about individuals can be inferred.
Third, homomorphic encryption.
This enables certain computations to be carried out on data while it remains encrypted.
Notice the qualification: it supports certain encrypted computations, not everything, and it comes with cost trade-offs.
Those costs, in practice, are things an organisation must weigh when deciding whether the approach is suitable.
Fourth, secure multiparty computation.
The source names it as a privacy-enhancing technology but gives no further detail, so we simply retain it in the list alongside the others.
Fifth, synthetic data.
This is artificial data created to stand in for real data.
The source warns that synthetic data can still reproduce identifying patterns.

Therefore, the organisation must evaluate leakage, that is, test whether the synthetic data still reveals information about real individuals, rather than assuming it is safe simply because it is artificial.
The source then lists further tools that can assist governance: zero-trust access, privacy-aware AI monitoring, automated data discovery, decentralised identity, and tamper-evident logs.
Zero-trust access means no user or system is trusted automatically; access is verified.
Automated data discovery helps an organisation find where personal data is held.
Tamper-evident logs make it apparent if records of activity have been altered.
The key qualification applies to all of these: they can assist governance, but they must be tested.
A tool that is purchased and deployed, but never tested, offers assurance on paper only.
Now to the second part of the chapter.
The source states that global harmonisation remains incomplete.
This means that laws and regulations on data protection still differ between countries and regions.
An organisation operating across borders cannot assume that one set of rules applies everywhere, and must pay attention to the requirements of each relevant jurisdiction.
Next, children's data, which requires special care.
The source identifies four elements.
First, age-appropriate notices, so that privacy information is understandable to the child concerned.
Second, minimisation, collecting only what is needed.
Third, guardian involvement where legally required.
Note the wording: the involvement of a parent or guardian is tied to what the law requires, and so it depends on the applicable jurisdiction.
Fourth, safeguards against exploitative profiling, so that children's data is not used to build profiles that take unfair advantage of them.
Finally, the source describes compliance as something never finished.

Organisations should maintain a continuous cycle with these elements, in this order: mapping, risk assessment, policy, controls, training, incident exercises, vendor reviews, rights handling, audit, and improvement.
Mapping means understanding what data you hold and where it flows.
Risk assessment identifies what could go wrong.
Policy sets the rules, and controls put them into practice.
Training prepares staff, and incident exercises test how the organisation responds when something goes wrong.
Vendor reviews examine the third parties that handle data on the organisation's behalf.
Rights handling means responding to individuals who exercise their data rights.
Audit checks that all of this is actually working, and improvement feeds the findings back into the start of the cycle.

The overall lesson of this chapter is that technology can strengthen privacy, but every tool has limits and must be evaluated and tested, while compliance depends on a continuing cycle of effort rather than a one-time project.
